scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): agrees that heroes reveal a society's ideals while arguing they do not reveal its whole character; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: The people a nation chooses to celebrate say a great deal about that nation.
One claim holds that the best way to understand a society's character is to examine its heroes, on the reason that heroes reveal a society's highest ideals.
I largely agree that heroes reveal a society's ideals, but I believe they do not reveal its whole character.
First, the reason behind the claim is sound, since heroes do reveal a society's ideals.
The qualities a society admires in its heroes show what it most deeply values.
For example, a nation that honours brave soldiers values courage above quiet comfort.
This shows that studying heroes can reveal a society's clearest hopes and beliefs.
The role models held up to children also shape the values of the next generation.
Whom a society celebrates is, in this way, a window into its ideals.
To this extent, the claim and its reason clearly hold.

sections.role: Body 2 — Why heroes are not the whole character

sentences.text: Second, however, heroes reveal a society's ideals but not its whole character.
What a society admires can be very different from how it actually behaves.
Consider a nation that praises noble heroes yet quietly mistreats its poor.
Such a gap shows that ideals and real conduct are not always the same.
A society's true character also appears in its laws, habits, and treatment of the weak.
People often admire heroes they have no real wish to imitate themselves.
Understanding a society, then, means looking beyond its heroes to its actions.
In conclusion, a society's heroes do reveal its highest ideals.
But its full character also shows in its laws, habits, and treatment of the weak.
We understand a society best by studying both whom it admires and how it truly acts.
